name: Coral Reef
description: Ecosystem engineering intelligence through distributed calcium carbonate construction and zooxanthellae photosynthetic symbiosis. Fractal branching structure dissipates wave energy while maximizing surface area for nutrient exchange. Creates biodiversity scaffolding — niche habitats supporting 25% of marine species from less than 1% of ocean floor. Bleaching-recovery cycles demonstrate symbiont strain switching as adaptive resilience.

core_attributes.pattern: symbiotic construction, fractal wave dissipation, biodiversity scaffolding

scope.definition: Fraction of coral host carbon demand supplied by photosynthate from symbiotic Symbiodinium algae (zooxanthellae) under optimal light and temperature conditions in shallow-water reef corals.

evidence.source: Muscatine & Porter (1977) 'Reef corals: mutualistic symbioses adapted to nutrient-poor environments', BioScience 27:454-460; Yellowlees et al. (2008) nutrient exchange review.
cross_domain_examples: zooxanthellae translocate 95% of fixed carbon to coral host in translocation experiments (Muscatine 1977)
coral bleaching at 30°C: zooxanthellae expelled, photosynthate supply drops to 0 within 2 weeks
lichen symbiosis: analogous photobiont-mycobiont carbon transfer, 60-70% of fungal carbon needs met
legume-rhizobium symbiosis: bacterial partner supplies 60-90% of plant nitrogen needs — N rather than C analogue

scope.falsifiability: If coral tissue isotope labeling shows <50% of carbon in host tissue is derived from zooxanthellae under optimal light, the near-complete autotrophy model is incorrect.
scope.measurement_limits: Photosynthetic contribution drops sharply with depth (light attenuation), water turbidity, and elevated temperature. Deep corals (>30 m) may only receive 30-50% of carbon from photosynthesis.

scope.definition: Fractal dimension (D) of three-dimensional reef structural complexity, compared to randomly-branching equivalent — higher D = greater structural complexity supporting biodiversity.

evidence.source: Bradbury & Reichelt (1983) 'Fractal dimension of a coral reef at ecological scales', Marine Ecology Progress Series 10:169-171; Zawada et al. (2019) 3D structure-function relationships in coral reefs.
cross_domain_examples: Great Barrier Reef structural fractal dimension D=2.7-2.9 across scales from 1 cm to 10 m
fractal dimension correlates with fish species richness R=0.82 across 23 Indo-Pacific reef sites
branching coral colonies independently optimize D for hydrodynamic drag reduction and feeding efficiency

scope.falsifiability: If artificially constructed reefs with identical material volume but non-fractal geometry support equivalent fish diversity, fractal complexity is not the diversity driver.
scope.measurement_limits: Fractal dimension measurement is scale-dependent and methodology varies between studies. Storm damage and bleaching reduce D by 0.3-0.8 units. Measurements from photogrammetric 3D models may underestimate fine-scale complexity.

scope.definition: Number of species supported per square meter of live reef surface compared to equivalent area of bare substrate — expressed as species density ratio.

evidence.source: Connell (1978) 'Diversity in tropical rain forests and coral reefs', Science 199:1302-1310; Bellwood & Hughes (2001) 'Regional-scale assembly rules and biodiversity of coral reefs', Science 292:1532-1535.
cross_domain_examples: healthy Indo-Pacific reef: 1000-3000 species per reef system, vs 0-20 on adjacent bare sand
species density on live coral: 0.5-2.0 species/cm² structural surface vs <0.01 on dead substrate
rainforest canopy: analogous structural complexity providing niche scaffolding for epiphytes and invertebrates
deep-sea chemosynthetic vents: biogenic structure (tube worm bushes) creating species-rich island in desert

scope.falsifiability: If coral reef biodiversity is statistically identical to adjacent seagrass meadows of equal area, structural complexity is not the primary biodiversity driver.
scope.measurement_limits: Niche scaffolding depends on live coral coverage — degraded reefs with <20% live cover show 60-80% species loss. Edge effects complicate per-area comparisons between reef zones.
